title: Highest Weight Theory for Complex Semisimple Lie Algebras

items.title: The roots form a reduced crystallographic Euclidean root system
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, root set $\Phi=\Phi(\mathfrak g,\mathfrak h)$ and Killing form $B$ ([[def-root-and-root-space-relative-to-a-cartan-subalgebra]], [[def-killing-form-of-a-finite-dimensional-lie-algebra]]). Let $$E:=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\Phi\subseteq\mathfrak h^* ,\qquad \mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}:=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{h_\alpha:\alpha\in\Phi\}$$ be the real span of the roots and the real span of the coroots ([[def-coroot-of-a-lie-algebra-root]]). Then: (i) every $\lambda\in E$ is real valued on $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$, and restriction is a linear isomorphism $E\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R},\mathbb R)$; (ii) $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$ is a real form of $\mathfrak h$, that is $\mathfrak h=\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}\oplus i\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$, and the Killing form restricted to $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$ is positive definite; (iii) the formula $$(\lambda,\mu):=B(H_\lambda,H_\mu)\qquad(\lambda,\mu\in E),$$ where $H_\lambda\in\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$ is the vector with $B(H_\lambda,H)=\lambda(H)$ for all $H\in\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$ ([[def-killing-dual-vector-of-a-root]]), defines a positive definite inner product on $E$, and for all roots $\alpha,\beta$ $$\frac{2(\beta,\alpha)}{(\alpha,\alpha)}=\beta(h_\alpha)\in\mathbb Z ;$$ (iv) with this inner product, $(E,\Phi)$ is a reduced crystallographic Euclidean root system in the sense of [[def-reduced-crystallographic-euclidean-root-system]], and for every root $\alpha$ the abstract reflection $x\mapsto x-\frac{2(x,\alpha)}{(\alpha,\alpha)}\alpha$ of that definition agrees with the reflection $s_\alpha(\lambda)=\lambda-\lambda(h_\alpha)\alpha$ of [[def-root-reflection-from-a-coroot]]; (v) if $\Delta=\{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r\}$ is the base of a positive system of $(E,\Phi)$ ([[def-positive-system-and-base-of-simple-roots]]), then $\Delta$ is a basis of $E$ and $\{h_{\alpha_1},\dots,h_{\alpha_r}\}$ is a basis of $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$, hence also a basis of $\mathfrak h$ over $\mathbb C$.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.
Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras

items.strategy: Build the real form from the coroots, show the Killing form is positive definite on it by the trace formula, transport it to the real span of the roots, and verify the Euclidean root-system axioms and the coroot basis.

items.title: Weight and weight space

references.title: Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras

items.title: Finite-dimensional modules decompose into weight spaces
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and let $V$ be a finite-dimensional representation of $\mathfrak g$ ([[def-representation-of-a-lie-algebra]]). Then $V$ is the direct sum of its weight spaces for $\mathfrak h$ ([[def-weight-and-weight-space-of-a-lie-algebra-representation]]): $$V=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\mathfrak h^*}V_\mu ,$$ and only finitely many of the spaces $V_\mu$ are nonzero.

references.title: Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras
Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: Restrict the representation to h. For each root alpha, the root sl2 triple makes every H_alpha act semisimply on V by the finite-dimensional sl2 theorem. Since the coroots span h and the operators rho(H) commute, every rho(H) is diagonalizable. Apply simultaneous diagonalization; the joint eigenspaces are exactly the V_mu and their sum is direct and exhaustive.

items.title: Simple reflections preserve weight multiplicities
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and root system $\Phi$, let $V$ be a finite-dimensional representation of $\mathfrak g$, and let $W$ be the Weyl group of $\Phi$, acting on $\mathfrak h^*$ by complex-linear extension of its action on $E=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\Phi$ ([[def-weyl-group-of-a-root-system]], [[prop-the-roots-form-a-reduced-crystallographic-euclidean-root-system]]). Then for every simple root $\alpha_i$ and every $\mu\in\mathfrak h^*$ $$\dim V_\mu=\dim V_{s_i(\mu)},\qquad s_i(\mu)=\mu-\mu(h_{\alpha_i})\alpha_i ,$$ and consequently $\dim V_{w\mu}=\dim V_\mu$ for every $w\in W$ and every $\mu\in\mathfrak h^*$ ([[def-weight-and-weight-space-of-a-lie-algebra-representation]]).

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.
Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras

items.strategy: Construct the invertible root-reflection operator exp(e_i)exp(-f_i)exp(e_i), compute its conjugation action on the Cartan, and use it to identify each weight space with its reflected weight space.

items.title: Root vectors shift weights
items.statement: Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, let $V$ be a representation of $\mathfrak g$, let $\alpha$ be a root and let $\mathfrak g_\alpha$ be its root space ([[def-root-and-root-space-relative-to-a-cartan-subalgebra]]). If $x\in\mathfrak g_\alpha$ and $v\in V_\mu$ for some $\mu\in\mathfrak h^*$, then $x\cdot v\in V_{\mu+\alpha}$ ([[def-weight-and-weight-space-of-a-lie-algebra-representation]]); in particular $x\cdot v=0$ is allowed.

references.title: Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras

items.strategy: For H in h compute H.(x.v)=[H,x].v+x.(H.v)=(alpha(H)+mu(H))x.v. Thus a nonzero x.v has the asserted joint eigenvalue.

items.title: Positive and negative nilpotent subalgebras and the Borel

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.title: Triangular decomposition
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a chosen positive system, and let $\mathfrak n^\pm$ and $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$ be as in [[def-positive-and-negative-nilpotent-subalgebras-and-borel-subalgebra]]. Then: (i) $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak n^-\oplus\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$ is a direct sum of vector spaces; (ii) $\mathfrak n^+$ and $\mathfrak n^-$ are nilpotent Lie subalgebras and $\mathfrak b$ is a solvable Lie subalgebra in which $\mathfrak n^+$ is an ideal, so that $\mathfrak b$ is the semidirect sum $\mathfrak h\ltimes\mathfrak n^+$.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: The root-space decomposition gives the direct sum. Brackets add roots, so a bracket of k positive-root spaces has height at least k and vanishes above the largest positive-root height; hence n+ is nilpotent, and similarly n-. The same bracket rule makes h+n+ closed, while its derived algebra lies in n+, so it is solvable.

items.title: Root order on weights

references.title: Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras
Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.title: Highest-weight vectors and modules

references.title: Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras
Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.title: Highest weight modules lie below the top weight
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a chosen positive system, and let $V$ be a representation generated by a highest weight vector $v$ of weight $\lambda$ ([[def-highest-weight-vector-and-highest-weight-module]]). Then $$V=U(\mathfrak n^-)v=U(\mathfrak n^-)\mathbb Cv ,$$ every weight $\mu$ of $V$ is of the form $\mu=\lambda-\sum_in_i\alpha_i$ with $n_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$, so that $\mu\le\lambda$ in the root order ([[def-partial-order-on-weights]]), and $$V_\lambda=\mathbb Cv .$$

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.
Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras

items.strategy: Use the PBW factorization U(g)=U(n^-)U(h)U(n^+) to write the module as U(n^-)Cv, compute weights of PBW monomials, and read off the lower bound and the top line.

items.title: Every finite-dimensional irreducible module has a highest-weight vector
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a chosen positive system, and let $V\ne0$ be a finite-dimensional irreducible representation of $\mathfrak g$ ([[def-irreducible-completely-reducible-and-faithful-lie-algebra-representation]]). Then $V$ contains a highest weight vector for the chosen positive roots ([[def-highest-weight-vector-and-highest-weight-module]]); consequently $V$ is a highest weight module for some highest weight $\lambda$.

references.title: Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras
Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: The finite set of weights has a maximal element lambda in root order. A nonzero v in V_lambda is killed by each positive root space, since otherwise the shift proposition would produce the larger weight lambda+alpha. Hence n+.v=0.

items.title: An irreducible module is generated by its highest-weight vector
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a chosen positive system, let $V$ be a finite-dimensional irreducible representation of $\mathfrak g$ ([[def-irreducible-completely-reducible-and-faithful-lie-algebra-representation]]), and let $v\in V$ be a highest weight vector ([[def-highest-weight-vector-and-highest-weight-module]]). Then the subrepresentation generated by $v$ is $V$; equivalently $U(\mathfrak g)v=V$.

references.title: Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras
Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: The enveloping-algebra span U(g)v is a nonzero g-submodule. Irreducibility leaves no proper nonzero submodule, so U(g)v=V.

items.title: The highest-weight space is one-dimensional
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a chosen positive system, and let $V$ be a finite-dimensional irreducible highest weight module of highest weight $\lambda$ ([[def-highest-weight-vector-and-highest-weight-module]]). Then the $\lambda$-weight space of $V$ is one-dimensional: $$\dim V_\lambda=1 .$$

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.
Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras

items.strategy: PBW orders every element of U(g) as a sum of products from U(n-)U(h)U(n+). On a highest vector, U(n+) acts by its augmentation and U(h) by the character lambda; every nonconstant U(n-) monomial lowers the weight. Thus the lambda-weight part of U(g)v is exactly Cv.

items.title: Integral, dominant, and strictly dominant weights

references.title: Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras
Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.title: Dominant weights in fundamental coordinates
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a chosen base of simple roots, and let $\omega_1,\dots,\omega_r$ be the fundamental weights ([[def-fundamental-weights]]). For $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$ the following are equivalent: (i) $\lambda$ is dominant integral ([[def-integral-dominant-and-strictly-dominant-weights]]); (ii) $\lambda=\sum_{i=1}^rn_i\omega_i$ with integers $n_i\ge0$.

references.title: Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras
Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: The simple coroots form the basis dual to the fundamental weights: lambda=sum_i <lambda,alpha_i^vee> omega_i. The coefficients are therefore nonnegative integers exactly under the dominant-integral inequalities.

items.title: Finite-dimensional highest weights are dominant integral
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a chosen positive system, and let $V$ be a finite-dimensional irreducible representation of $\mathfrak g$. Then the highest weight of $V$ is dominant integral ([[def-integral-dominant-and-strictly-dominant-weights]]).

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.
Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras

items.strategy: For each simple root alpha_i, restrict to its sl2 triple. The highest vector is killed by e_i and has h_i-eigenvalue <lambda,alpha_i^vee>. The finite-dimensional sl2 string theorem makes that eigenvalue a nonnegative integer. Do this for every i.

items.title: Simple-root integrability relations
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a chosen positive system with simple roots $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r$, let $\lambda$ be dominant integral with $m_i=\langle\lambda,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle$ ([[def-integral-dominant-and-strictly-dominant-weights]]), and let $V$ be a finite-dimensional highest weight module of highest weight $\lambda$ with highest weight vector $v_\lambda$ ([[def-highest-weight-vector-and-highest-weight-module]]). For every simple root $\alpha_i$ and a lowering vector $f_i\in\mathfrak g_{-\alpha_i}$ with $[e_i,f_i]=h_{\alpha_i}$ for a suitable $e_i$ ([[thm-root-sl-two-triple]]), $$f_i^{\,m_i+1}v_\lambda=0 .$$

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.
Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras

source_locators: §8.3, Step 1 of the proof of Theorem 8.23
items.strategy: Restrict the cyclic vector to the simple-root sl2. It is a highest vector of integer weight m_i; the explicit finite sl2 string has length m_i+1, so the next lowering vector is zero.

items.title: Dominant integrable cyclic highest-weight module

references.title: Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras
Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.title: The dominant cyclic generator survives
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a chosen positive system, let $\lambda$ be dominant integral, and let $M_{\mathrm{int}}(\lambda)=U(\mathfrak g)/I_\lambda$ be the cyclic module with canonical generator $v_\lambda$ of [[def-dominant-integrable-highest-weight-cyclic-module]]. Then $$v_\lambda\ne0 ,$$ $v_\lambda$ is a weight vector of weight $\lambda$, and $\mathfrak n^+\cdot v_\lambda=0$.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.
Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras

source_locators: §8.3, Step 1–2 of the proof of Theorem 8.23
items.strategy: First quotient U(g) only by n+ and the relations H-lambda(H). PBW identifies this induced module with U(n-)v_lambda, so v_lambda is nonzero and its top weight line is one-dimensional. For m_i=<lambda,alpha_i^vee>, the rank-one identity e_i f_i^r v=r(m_i-r+1)f_i^(r-1)v makes f_i^(m_i+1)v singular; for j≠i the Chevalley relations give [e_j,f_i]=0, so all of n+ kills it. Its generated submodule is U(n-)f_i^(m_i+1)v and has weights strictly below lambda. Therefore the sum of these submodules misses the top line, and quotienting by it leaves a nonzero highest generator with the asserted relations.

items.title: Simple-root integrability bounds the dominant cyclic module
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a chosen positive system, and let $\lambda$ be dominant integral. Then the cyclic module $M_{\mathrm{int}}(\lambda)$ of [[def-dominant-integrable-highest-weight-cyclic-module]] is finite-dimensional.

references.title: Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras
Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: PBW makes e_i locally nilpotent because all weights are bounded above in lambda-Q_+. The defining relation makes f_i locally nilpotent on v_lambda; the Serre/root-string relations make ad(f_i) locally nilpotent on U(n-), and the binomial commutator identity for f_i^N u.v_lambda propagates local nilpotence to every PBW vector. Thus each simple-root sl2 action is integrable, and its finite strings show that simple reflections preserve weights and their multiplicities. Every weight lies in lambda-Q_+, so Weyl invariance places it in the intersection over w of w(lambda-Q_+); the corresponding finite family of chamber inequalities is bounded by the Weyl orbit of lambda, and its lattice intersection is finite. Finally, for a fixed beta in Q_+, only finitely many ordered positive-root PBW monomials have total weight beta, so each weight space is finite-dimensional. Hence the whole cyclic module is finite-dimensional.

items.title: Unique simple quotient of the dominant cyclic module
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a chosen positive system, let $\lambda$ be dominant integral, and let $M=M_{\mathrm{int}}(\lambda)$ with canonical generator $v_\lambda$ ([[def-dominant-integrable-highest-weight-cyclic-module]]). Then $M$ has a unique maximal proper submodule $N_\lambda$, and the quotient $$L(\lambda):=M/N_\lambda$$ is a nonzero simple $\mathfrak g$-module; in particular $M$ has, up to isomorphism, a unique simple quotient.

references.title: Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras
Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: The PBW-survival lemma gives a one-dimensional top line Cv_lambda. Every proper submodule misses it, since containing v_lambda would generate the whole cyclic module; because submodules are weight-space sums, each has zero lambda-weight space. Their sum therefore still misses Cv_lambda and is proper. It contains every proper submodule and is the unique maximal one. The quotient is simple and retains its nonzero highest line.

items.title: Dominant simple highest-weight modules are finite-dimensional
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a chosen positive system, and let $\lambda$ be dominant integral. Then the simple module $L(\lambda)$ of [[lem-a-dominant-cyclic-highest-weight-module-has-a-unique-simple-quotient]] is finite-dimensional and is a simple highest weight module of highest weight $\lambda$.

references.title: Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras
Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: The module L(lambda) is the quotient of the finite-dimensional module M_int(lambda), so it is finite-dimensional.

items.title: Simple highest-weight modules are classified by highest weight
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a fixed positive system. Then two finite-dimensional simple highest weight $\mathfrak g$-modules for this positive system are isomorphic if and only if their highest weights are equal.

references.title: Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras
Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: An isomorphism preserves h-weights, so it preserves the unique top weight. Conversely, two simple modules with top weight lambda satisfy the same cyclic highest-weight and simple-root integrability relations, hence are simple quotients of M_int(lambda); uniqueness of that quotient identifies them.

items.title: Highest-weight classification
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a fixed positive system. Then the maps $$V\longmapsto\lambda(V),\qquad \lambda\longmapsto L(\lambda)$$ are mutually inverse bijections between the isomorphism classes of finite-dimensional irreducible representations of $\mathfrak g$ and the dominant integral weights ([[def-integral-dominant-and-strictly-dominant-weights]]); here $\lambda(V)$ is the highest weight of $V$ ([[def-highest-weight-vector-and-highest-weight-module]]) and $L(\lambda)$ is the simple quotient of $M_{\mathrm{int}}(\lambda)$.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.
Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras

items.strategy: Existence of a top vector and the rank-one test send every finite-dimensional irreducible to a dominant integral weight. The finite-dimensional construction gives an irreducible for every such weight, and uniqueness by highest weight proves injectivity and exhaustivity.

items.title: Every finite-dimensional module is a direct sum of highest-weight modules
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a fixed positive system. Then every finite-dimensional representation $V$ of $\mathfrak g$ is a finite direct sum $V=V_1\oplus\dots\oplus V_N$ of irreducible submodules, where each $V_j$ is isomorphic to a highest-weight module $L(\lambda_j)$ for a dominant integral weight $\lambda_j$ ([[def-integral-dominant-and-strictly-dominant-weights]]).

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.
Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras

items.strategy: Weyl complete reducibility splits the representation into irreducible summands. Apply the highest-weight classification to each summand.

items.title: Highest weight of the dual representation
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a fixed positive system, let $\lambda$ be dominant integral, let $V(\lambda)=L(\lambda)$ be the finite-dimensional irreducible module of highest weight $\lambda$, and let $w_0$ be the longest element of the Weyl group ([[def-length-and-longest-element-of-a-finite-weyl-group]]). Then the dual module $V(\lambda)^*$ ([[prop-direct-sum-dual-hom-and-tensor-representations]]) is irreducible and has highest weight $$-w_0(\lambda).$$

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.
Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras

items.strategy: The dual weights are negatives of the weights of V. Successive finite sl2 strings show that the weight set and multiplicities are Weyl-invariant. The longest element sends the chosen chamber to its negative, so w0(lambda) is the unique lowest extremal weight; its space has the same dimension as the top line, namely one. Its negative is therefore the unique highest weight of V*, and dual irreducibility follows from annihilators.

items.title: Top summand in a tensor product
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a fixed positive system, and let $\lambda,\mu$ be dominant integral weights ([[def-integral-dominant-and-strictly-dominant-weights]]). Then the tensor product $V(\lambda)\otimes V(\mu)$ ([[prop-direct-sum-dual-hom-and-tensor-representations]]) contains $V(\lambda+\mu)$ as a summand with multiplicity one, and every other irreducible summand has highest weight strictly below $\lambda+\mu$ in the root order ([[def-partial-order-on-weights]]).

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.
Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras

items.strategy: The tensor of top vectors is a highest vector of weight lambda+mu. All tensor weights are sums of weights lying below lambda and mu, so none exceeds lambda+mu. The top weight space is the tensor of the two one-dimensional top lines and is one-dimensional; complete reducibility therefore gives exactly one V(lambda+mu), with every other top weight lower.

items.title: The adjoint highest weight is the highest root
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex simple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a fixed positive system whose highest root is $\theta$ ([[def-height-of-a-root-and-highest-root]]). Then the adjoint representation of $\mathfrak g$ on itself ([[def-adjoint-representation-of-a-lie-algebra]]) is irreducible, and its highest weight is $\theta$.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.
Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras

items.strategy: Submodules of the adjoint module are ideals, so simplicity gives irreducibility. Its nonzero weights are exactly the roots and its zero-weight space is h. A vector in g_theta is killed by every positive root space because theta+alpha is no root, hence is a top vector; maximality of theta identifies the highest weight.

items.title: The Weyl vector

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.
Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras

items.title: The Weyl vector in fundamental coordinates
items.statement: Let $\Phi\subseteq E$ be a reduced crystallographic root system with positive system $\Phi^+$, base $\Delta=\{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r\}$ and Weyl vector $\rho$ ([[def-weyl-vector-rho]]). Then $$(\rho,\alpha_i^\vee)=1\qquad(i=1,\dots,r),$$ and therefore $$\rho=\sum_{i=1}^r\omega_i ,$$ where $\omega_1,\dots,\omega_r$ are the fundamental weights ([[def-fundamental-weights]]).

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.
Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras

items.strategy: The simple reflection s_i permutes Delta+ except that it sends alpha_i to -alpha_i. Thus s_i(rho)=rho-alpha_i. Comparing with s_i(rho)=rho-<rho,alpha_i^vee>alpha_i gives the pairing 1. The defining duality of fundamental weights then yields the sum.

items.title: Extremal Weyl-orbit weights
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a fixed positive system with Weyl group $W$ and fundamental chamber $C$ ([[def-open-and-closed-weyl-chambers]], [[thm-the-weyl-group-acts-simply-transitively-on-weyl-chambers]]), let $\lambda$ be dominant integral, and let $V(\lambda)$ be the finite-dimensional irreducible module of highest weight $\lambda$. Then for every $w\in W$ the weight $w(\lambda)$ occurs in $V(\lambda)$ with multiplicity one, $$\dim V(\lambda)_{w(\lambda)}=1 ,$$ and $w(\lambda)$ is extremal in the chamber $w(C)$, in the following sense: every weight $\mu$ of $V(\lambda)$ satisfies $w^{-1}(\mu)\le\lambda$ in the root order, equivalently $w(\lambda)-\mu$ is a nonnegative integral combination of the positive roots of the positive system defined by the chamber $w(C)$.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.
Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras

items.strategy: For a simple reflection, the complete finite sl2 string through a weight reverses its endpoints and preserves endpoint multiplicities. Starting with the one-dimensional top line and following a reduced expression for w produces w(lambda) with multiplicity one. The same string inequalities transport dominance to the chamber w(C+), proving extremality there.

items.title: Beyond finite-dimensional highest-weight theory

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.title: Not every weight vector is highest
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every weight vector in a finite-dimensional module over a complex semisimple Lie algebra is a highest weight vector.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: In the standard two-dimensional sl2 module, the lower basis vector is a weight vector and the positive root vector sends it to the nonzero upper vector. It is therefore not highest.

items.title: Verma modules need not be finite-dimensional
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every Verma module for a complex semisimple Lie algebra is finite-dimensional.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.
Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras

items.strategy: For sl2, induce from a Borel character. PBW gives the linearly independent vectors f^n v for every n>=0, so the module is infinite-dimensional.

items.title: Finite-dimensionality requires dominance integrality
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every functional $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$ is the highest weight of a finite-dimensional simple module over the complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: Choose lambda with <lambda,alpha_i^vee> not a nonnegative integer. The rank-one necessity lemma rules out any finite-dimensional simple module with that highest weight.

items.title: Dominance depends on a positive system
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Dominance of weights is defined canonically, without choosing positive roots.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: For sl2, choosing alpha positive makes lambda dominant when <lambda,alpha^vee>>=0; choosing -alpha positive reverses the inequality. A nonzero integral lambda cannot satisfy the same designation under both choices.

items.title: A tensor-product top weight does not determine all constituents
items.statement: The highest weight of a tensor product $V\otimes W$ of finite-dimensional irreducible modules over a complex semisimple Lie algebra determines the complete irreducible decomposition of $V\otimes W$.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.
Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras

items.strategy: For sl2, V(1) tensor V(1) and V(2) both have top weight 2, but the first has dimension 4 and contains an invariant alternating line while V(2) has dimension 3. Thus top weight determines only the top summand.

items.title: The Weyl quotient requires cancellation or extension
items.statement: In the Weyl character formula the numerator divided by the denominator is an ordinary pointwise quotient on the whole torus before any cancellation or continuous extension is justified.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.
Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras

items.strategy: Already for SU(2), numerator and denominator both vanish at the identity. The displayed quotient is 0/0 there; it becomes a character only after algebraic cancellation on the regular set and continuous extension.

title: Highest Weight Theory for Complex Semisimple Lie Algebras — Examples

items.title: All irreducible finite-dimensional sl2 modules
items.statement: Let $\mathfrak{sl}_2=\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ have its standard basis $e,f,h$ with $[e,f]=h$, $[h,e]=2e$, $[h,f]=-2f$ ([[def-special-linear-lie-algebra-sl-two]]). For every integer $n\ge0$ let $V(n)$ be the vector space with basis $v_0,v_1,\dots,v_n$ and let $$h\cdot v_k=(n-2k)v_k,\qquad f\cdot v_k=v_{k+1},\qquad e\cdot v_k=k(n-k+1)v_{k-1},$$ where $v_{-1}=v_{n+1}=0$. Then: (i) these formulas define a representation of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ on $V(n)$; (ii) $V(n)$ is irreducible of dimension $n+1$; (iii) every finite-dimensional irreducible $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-module is isomorphic to exactly one $V(n)$.

references.title: Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras
Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: Verify the three sl2 brackets on the displayed basis. Any nonzero submodule contains a weight vector; repeated e reaches v_0, then repeated f spans the basis, proving irreducibility. The rank-one highest-weight classification says every irreducible has one of the nonnegative integer top weights n and hence is this module.

items.title: Verma modules for sl2
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak{sl}_2=\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ have basis $e,f,h$ with $[e,f]=h$, $[h,e]=2e$, $[h,f]=-2f$ ([[def-special-linear-lie-algebra-sl-two]]), and for every complex number $\lambda$ let $M(\lambda)$ be the induced module $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)\otimes_{U(\mathbb Ch\oplus\mathbb Ce)}\mathbb C_\lambda$, realised concretely as $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)/J_\lambda$ with $J_\lambda$ the left ideal generated by $e$ and $h-\lambda(h)$ ([[def-universal-enveloping-algebra]], [[def-highest-weight-vector-and-highest-weight-module]]). Then $M(\lambda)$ has basis $v_k=f^k\cdot v_0$, $k\ge0$, on which $$h\cdot v_k=(\lambda(h)-2k)v_k,\qquad f\cdot v_k=v_{k+1},\qquad e\cdot v_k=k(\lambda(h)-k+1)v_{k-1};$$ it is infinite-dimensional, and it has a finite-dimensional simple quotient exactly when $\lambda(h)$ is a nonnegative integer. In that case the quotient is $V(n)$ of [[ex-all-finite-dimensional-irreducible-sl-two-modules]] with $n=\lambda(h)$.

references.title: Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras
Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: Check the brackets directly and use PBW to identify v_k=f^k v_0 as a basis. The coefficient of e.v_k vanishes for k=lambda+1 exactly when lambda is a nonnegative integer; then the tail it generates is the unique maximal submodule and the quotient is V(lambda). Otherwise every nonzero submodule raised by e reaches v_0, so the Verma module is simple and infinite.

items.title: Standard and dual representations of sl_n
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge2$, $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb C):\operatorname{tr}A=0\}$ ([[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]]), let $\mathfrak h$ be the diagonal traceless matrices, let $\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_n\in\mathfrak h^*$ be the coordinate functionals $\varepsilon_i(H)=H_{ii}$, and let the positive system be the roots $\varepsilon_i-\varepsilon_j$ with $i<j$, with base $\alpha_j=\varepsilon_j-\varepsilon_{j+1}$ ([[prop-root-systems-of-the-classical-complex-lie-algebras]]). Then the standard module $\mathbb C^n$ with its natural action is irreducible of highest weight $\omega_1=\varepsilon_1$, and its dual is irreducible of highest weight $\omega_{n-1}=-\varepsilon_n$ ([[def-fundamental-weights]]).

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.
Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras

items.strategy: Diagonal matrices give weights epsilon_i modulo their sum. The upper root matrices kill e_1, so its weight is omega_1. In the dual, they kill e_n^*, whose weight is -epsilon_n=omega_{n-1}; the matrix units generate each module from that line, proving irreducibility.

items.title: Symmetric powers as highest-weight modules
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)$ with its diagonal Cartan $\mathfrak h$, coordinate functionals $\varepsilon_i$ and upper-triangular positive system as in [[ex-standard-and-dual-representations-of-sl-n-by-highest-weights]]. For every $m\ge1$ the symmetric power $\operatorname{Sym}^m(\mathbb C^n)$ is an irreducible module of highest weight $m\omega_1$.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

source_locators: Chapter V §1 examples and Chapter I §3
items.strategy: Identify Sym^m(C^n) with homogeneous degree-m polynomials, so E_ij acts as x_i partial_j. The degree-m monomials have pairwise distinct sl_n weights, and polynomial projections in finitely many diagonal Cartan operators therefore isolate a nonzero monomial x_1^{a_1}...x_n^{a_n} in every nonzero submodule U. Applying E_{1j}^{a_j} successively for j>1 gives a nonzero multiple of x_1^m, so x_1^m lies in U. This monomial is killed by all upper root matrices and has weight m omega_1. Conversely, for any exponents summing to m, applying E_{j1}^{a_j} successively to x_1^m gives a nonzero factorial multiple of the corresponding monomial. Hence U contains the complete monomial basis and is the whole module. This proves irreducibility directly, with no assumed highest vector or irreducible summand. AC is inherited through the preceding highest-weight conventions, not used in these finite polynomial manipulations.

items.title: Exterior powers and fundamental weights of sl_n
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)$ with its diagonal Cartan $\mathfrak h$, coordinate functionals $\varepsilon_i$ and upper-triangular positive system as in [[ex-standard-and-dual-representations-of-sl-n-by-highest-weights]]. For every $k$ with $1\le k\le n-1$ the exterior power $\Lambda^k(\mathbb C^n)$ is an irreducible module of highest weight $\omega_k=\varepsilon_1+\dots+\varepsilon_k$ ([[def-fundamental-weights]]).

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.
Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras

items.strategy: The ordered wedges e_I=e_{i_1}∧...∧e_{i_k} are a weight basis with pairwise distinct weights for k<n. Polynomial projections in finitely many diagonal Cartan operators therefore put some e_I in every nonzero submodule U. Applying raising matrix units that replace a selected index by a smaller missing index, with the exterior sign and no cancellation, reaches e_1∧...∧e_k; hence that highest vector lies in U. It is killed by all upper root matrices and has weight epsilon_1+...+epsilon_k=omega_k. Conversely successive lowering replacements generate every e_I from it. Thus U contains the whole wedge basis and the module is irreducible, without invoking complete reducibility or an unproved irreducible summand. AC is inherited only through the preceding highest-weight conventions.

items.title: The adjoint representation and highest root
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)$ with $n\ge2$, its diagonal Cartan $\mathfrak h$, coordinate functionals $\varepsilon_i$ and upper-triangular positive system, the adjoint representation has highest vector $E_{1n}$ and highest weight $\varepsilon_1-\varepsilon_n$, which is the highest root ([[def-adjoint-representation-of-a-lie-algebra]], [[def-height-of-a-root-and-highest-root]]).

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.
Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras

items.strategy: Commuting a diagonal matrix with E_1n gives weight epsilon_1-epsilon_n. Every positive root matrix commutes with E_1n or has an out-of-range matrix index, so it kills this vector; the displayed root is the unique maximum among positive roots.

items.title: Weyl character and dimension formulas for sl2
items.statement: For the finite-dimensional irreducible $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-module $V(n)$ with basis $v_0,\dots,v_n$ of [[ex-all-finite-dimensional-irreducible-sl-two-modules]], put $$\chi_n(z)=\sum_{k=0}^nz^{n-2k}=z^n+z^{n-2}+\dots+z^{-n}\qquad(z\in\mathbb C^\times).$$ Then for $z\ne\pm1$ $$\chi_n(z)=\frac{z^{n+1}-z^{-(n+1)}}{z-z^{-1}},$$ and $$\dim V(n)=n+1 .$$

references.title: Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras
Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: The explicit finite weight string gives the finite Laurent sum. Multiplying it by z-z^{-1} telescopes to the numerator, so no Weyl-character theorem is used. Cancelling first and then setting z=1 gives n+1.

items.title: The eight-dimensional adjoint representation of sl3
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. The adjoint representation of $\mathfrak{sl}_3(\mathbb C)$ has dimension $8$, highest weight $\alpha_1+\alpha_2=\omega_1+\omega_2$, six one-dimensional root-weight spaces, and a two-dimensional zero-weight space.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.
Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras

items.strategy: Use the six off-diagonal matrix units E_ij as root vectors and the two-dimensional traceless diagonal Cartan as weight zero. E_13 has root alpha_1+alpha_2 and is killed by the positive root spaces. Counting gives dimension 6+2=8.

items.title: Clebsch–Gordan decomposition for sl2
items.statement: For integers $a,b\ge0$ and the irreducible $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-modules $V(a)$, $V(b)$ of [[ex-all-finite-dimensional-irreducible-sl-two-modules]], $$V(a)\otimes V(b)\cong\bigoplus_{i=0}^{\min(a,b)}V(a+b-2i),$$ each summand occurring with multiplicity one.

references.title: Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras
Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: Use the explicit finite strings to compute the tensor character as (sum_{r=0}^a x^{a-2r})(sum_{s=0}^b x^{b-2s}). A direct diagonal count and telescoping show it equals sum_{j=0}^{min(a,b)} sum_{k=0}^{a+b-2j} x^{a+b-2j-2k}. Complete reducibility and uniqueness of sl2 highest weights turn this character identity into the stated multiplicity-one direct sum. This is a local finite-string proof, not a dependency on the later representation-learning page.

items.title: A nondominant integral highest-weight module can be infinite-dimensional
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. If a functional $\lambda$ is integral, then the highest weight module $M(\lambda)$ of weight $\lambda$ is finite-dimensional.

references.title: Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras
Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: In the displayed Verma action e.v_k=k(-k)v_{k-1}, which is nonzero for every k>0. Any nonzero submodule therefore raises to v_0 and is all of M(-1), so the module is simple. Its PBW basis is infinite, while <-1,alpha^vee>=-1 makes the weight integral but not dominant.

items.title: The full weight lattice need not integrate through a central quotient
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every dominant weight in the weight lattice of a compact semisimple group integrates to every compact group form with the given Lie algebra.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.
Alexander Kirillov Jr., An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras

items.strategy: In V(n), the central matrix -I in SU(2) acts on the highest vector, hence on the irreducible module, by (-1)^n. A representation factors through SU(2)/{±I}=SO(3) exactly when this kernel element acts trivially. Thus n=1 does not descend and precisely the even n do. The calculation is explicit and uses no later compact-group classification theorem.

title: Compact Lie Groups Maximal Tori and Peter Weyl Theory

items.title: Left, right, and bi-invariant Borel measures
items.statement: A finite Radon measure mu on a Lie group G is left invariant when mu(gE)=mu(E), right invariant when mu(Eg)=mu(E), and bi-invariant when both hold, for all Borel E and g; equivalently its integral on C(G) is unchanged by the corresponding translations.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.title: Normalized Haar measure on a compact Lie group
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every compact Lie group has a unique regular Borel probability measure invariant under left and right translations and inversion.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: Apply the published compact-group Haar corollary to the underlying compact Hausdorff group. Its uniqueness gives right invariance by comparing a right translate with the normalized left Haar measure, and inversion carries left Haar to right Haar; uniqueness identifies all three.

items.title: Haar integration is translation and conjugation invariant
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For normalized Haar measure dg and integrable f, the integrals of f(gx), f(xg), f(gxg^{-1}), and f(x^{-1}) all equal the integral of f.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: Left, right, and inversion invariance give the first, second, and fourth equalities by change of variables. Compose a left and a right translation for conjugation. Extend from continuous functions to integrable functions using equality of the pushed-forward regular Borel measures.

items.title: Continuous and unitary representations
items.statement: A finite-dimensional complex representation of a compact Lie group is a continuous homomorphism pi:G→GL(V); it is unitary relative to a Hermitian inner product when every pi(g) preserves that inner product. Infinite-dimensional Hilbert representations are named explicitly when used.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.title: Finite-dimensional compact-group representations are unitarizable
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every finite-dimensional continuous complex representation of a compact Lie group preserves some positive-definite Hermitian inner product.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: Begin with any Hermitian product ( , )_0 and define <v,w>=∫_G (pi(g)v,pi(g)w)_0 dg. Positivity follows because a nonzero v has a continuous strictly positive integrand at the identity, and left invariance gives <pi(h)v,pi(h)w>=<v,w>.

items.title: Complete reducibility for compact Lie groups
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every finite-dimensional continuous complex representation of a compact Lie group is a direct sum of irreducible representations.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: For an invariant subspace W, its orthogonal complement under an invariant inner product is invariant. Induct on dimension, splitting off an irreducible subspace and then its invariant complement.

items.title: Matrix coefficients and characters
items.statement: For pi on V, a matrix coefficient is g↦<pi(g)v,w>; the character is chi_pi(g)=tr(pi(g)).

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.title: Schur orthogonality
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For irreducible unitary pi and sigma of dimensions d_pi,d_sigma and orthonormal bases, ∫ pi_ij(g) overline{sigma_kl(g)} dg is zero if pi and sigma are inequivalent and equals delta_ik delta_jl/d_pi if they are equivalent under the fixed identification.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: Average the rank-one map u↦<u,e_l>e_j as ∫ pi(g)A sigma(g)^{-1}dg. It intertwines sigma and pi. The elementary Schur argument makes it zero for inequivalent irreducibles and scalar for an irreducible endomorphism; taking traces determines the scalar and yields the displayed indices.

items.title: Irreducible characters are orthonormal class functions
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Characters of pairwise inequivalent irreducible unitary representations are orthonormal in L2(G), and every character is conjugation invariant.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: Trace is invariant under conjugation. Expand each character as the sum of diagonal matrix coefficients and apply Schur orthogonality; the d diagonal contributions each have norm square 1/d.

items.title: Compact Lie groups admit bi-invariant metrics
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every compact Lie group admits a Riemannian metric invariant under both left and right translations; for such a metric, geodesics through the identity are precisely one-parameter subgroups.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: Average any inner product on g over Ad(G). Left-translate it to a metric; Ad-invariance is exactly the condition that right translations are isometries. The Koszul formula for left-invariant fields gives nabla_X Y=(1/2)[X,Y], so nabla_X X=0 and exp(tX) is geodesic; uniqueness of geodesics gives the converse through the identity.

items.title: Tori and maximal tori
items.statement: A torus is a compact connected abelian Lie group. A maximal torus of G is a torus subgroup maximal under inclusion.

references.title: Brian Conrad and Aaron Landesman, Compact Lie Groups

items.title: Structure of compact connected abelian Lie groups
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. If T is compact, connected, and abelian with Lie algebra t, then exp:t→T is surjective, its kernel Lambda is a full lattice, and T is isomorphic to t/Lambda and to (S1)^r.

references.title: Brian Conrad and Aaron Landesman, Compact Lie Groups

items.strategy: The exponential is a local diffeomorphism and a homomorphism because t is abelian, so its image is an open subgroup and hence all of connected T. The kernel is discrete. Compactness of t/Lambda forces Lambda to span t; choosing a lattice basis identifies the quotient with R^r/Z^r and hence with (S1)^r.

items.title: Existence of maximal tori
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every compact Lie group contains a maximal torus, and every torus is contained in one.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: Among connected abelian Lie subgroups containing a given torus, choose one of maximal dimension (bounded by dim G). If it were not closed, the identity component of its closure would be a connected compact abelian subgroup with strictly larger Lie algebra. Its closure is therefore a torus, and any proper torus enlargement would increase dimension, proving maximality.

items.title: Every element lies in a maximal torus
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every element of a compact connected Lie group belongs to a maximal torus.

references.title: Brian Conrad and Aaron Landesman, Compact Lie Groups

items.strategy: Compactness makes the bi-invariant metric complete. Hopf–Rinow gives a minimizing geodesic from the identity to g. Left-translate its initial velocity to X in g; the bi-invariant geodesic calculation makes the path exp(tX), so g=exp X. The closure of exp(RX) is connected (as the closure of a connected set), compact, and abelian, hence a torus containing g, and the maximal-torus existence theorem enlarges it. This includes finite-order g without taking the identity component of its cyclic closure.

items.title: Conjugacy of maximal tori
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Any two maximal tori of a compact connected Lie group are conjugate.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: Their Lie algebras are maximal abelian: otherwise the closure of the analytic subgroup of a larger abelian algebra enlarges the torus. Choose regular X and Y in the two algebras, avoiding the finitely many root hyperplanes, so their Lie-algebra centralizers are exactly those algebras. Compactness gives g minimizing <Ad(g)X,Y>. Differentiation in exp(sZ)g and invariance of the averaged inner product yield <Z,[Ad(g)X,Y]>=0 for all Z, hence the bracket vanishes. Thus the first maximal abelian algebra lies in the centralizer of Ad(g)X, namely Ad(g) of the second, and maximality gives equality; connected analytic subgroups then give conjugacy of the tori.

items.title: Connected abelian subgroups lie in maximal tori
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every compact connected abelian subgroup of a compact Lie group is contained in a maximal torus.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: Such a subgroup is a torus by definition, so apply the containing form of maximal-torus existence.

items.title: Rank is well-defined
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. All maximal tori of a compact connected Lie group have the same dimension; this common dimension is the rank of G.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: Conjugation is a Lie-group isomorphism and preserves dimension, so conjugate maximal tori have equal dimension.

items.title: Compact Weyl group
items.statement: For a compact connected G and maximal torus T, the Weyl group is W(G,T)=N_G(T)/T.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.title: The compact Weyl group is finite
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. The centralizer of every torus S in a compact connected Lie group is connected; in particular C_G(T)=T for a maximal torus T. Consequently W(G,T) is finite and acts faithfully on T and its Lie algebra.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: Let S be any torus and g in C_G(S). The compact abelian closure A of the subgroup generated by g and S has cyclic component group. Its identity component is a torus; the dense-cyclic-element lemma for such A and surjectivity of exp in connected compact G put A inside the closure of a one-parameter subgroup, hence inside a torus S' containing S and g. Therefore C_G(S) is the union of the connected tori containing S, all meeting in S, so C_G(S) is connected. For maximal T this also gives C_G(T)=T. Thus conjugation embeds N_G(T)/T into Aut(T). Its Lie algebra is zero because the normalizer algebra equals the centralizer algebra t, so the quotient is discrete; it is compact, hence finite. The equality C_G(T)=T proves faithfulness.

items.title: Conjugacy classes meet T in Weyl orbits
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every conjugacy class meets T, and two points of T are conjugate in G exactly when they lie in the same W(G,T)-orbit.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: The first assertion follows by putting an element in some maximal torus and conjugating that torus to T. If t'=gtg^{-1} lies in T, then T and gTg^{-1} are maximal tori of the connected centralizer C_G(t')^0. The centralizer-of-a-torus argument places them there and conjugacy inside that group gives h centralizing t' with hg normalizing T; hence t' is a Weyl conjugate of t. The converse is immediate.

items.title: Roots of a compact connected Lie group
items.statement: For maximal torus T with complexified Lie algebra t_C, the roots are the nonzero characters alpha:T→S1 occurring in the complexified adjoint representation on g_C; their differentials are also denoted alpha.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.title: Compact roots form a reduced crystallographic root system
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. The roots of (G,T) vanish on the central torus and form a reduced crystallographic root system on the dual of the semisimple part of t.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: The Ad-invariant positive inner product splits the compact Lie algebra orthogonally as its center plus its derived semisimple ideal. Complexification makes t_C the center plus a Cartan subalgebra of the derived algebra. The adjoint action is trivial on the center, while its nonzero T-weights differentiate to exactly the Lie-algebra roots on the semisimple summand. Apply the audited reduced crystallographic root-system theorem there.

items.title: Analytic and root-system Weyl groups agree
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. The faithful action of W(G,T) on the semisimple part of t identifies it with the Weyl group generated by the root reflections. For every root alpha the corresponding compact root SU(2) supplies a cocharacter alpha^vee:S1→T with <alpha,alpha^vee>=2, and conjugation by its standard normalizer element acts by s_alpha.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: Choose a root vector E_alpha and normalize it against compact conjugation as in Knapp. The real span of E_alpha+bar(E_alpha), i(E_alpha-bar(E_alpha)), and iH_alpha is su(2); Lie's second theorem integrates this homomorphism from simply connected SU(2) to G. Its diagonal circle defines alpha^vee:S1→T, gives <alpha,alpha^vee>=2, and the standard SU(2) normalizer element acts on t by s_alpha. Hence the root Weyl group lies in W(G,T). Conversely let g be represented in N_G(T). Choose a root-Weyl element w such that wg carries the chosen positive chamber to itself. It may permute, rather than fix, the simple roots; what it necessarily fixes is rho, the half-sum of the positive roots. A representative of wg therefore centralizes the torus S=closure(exp(i R H_rho)). Since <rho,alpha_i^vee>=1, rho is regular and the root-space decomposition gives Lie(C_G(S))=t. Prove C_G(S) connected locally and noncircularly. For x in C_G(S), the torus-containment theorem puts x in a torus of G, hence in C_G(x)^0; connectedness of S also puts S in C_G(x)^0. Inside the compact connected group C_G(x)^0 choose a maximal torus T' containing S. The element x is central there and lies in one maximal torus; conjugacy of maximal tori therefore puts x in every maximal torus, in particular T'. Since T' is connected and centralizes S, x lies in C_G(S)^0. Thus C_G(S) is connected. Its Lie algebra is t, so C_G(S)=T. Hence wg is trivial in N_G(T)/T, proving the reverse inclusion without a disconnected-abelian-subgroup claim, a circular Weyl equality, or the false chamber-fixing inference.

items.title: Weyl Jacobian
items.statement: For positive roots Delta+, define J(t)=product_{alpha>0}|1-alpha(t)^{-1}|^2 on T. Each root is an actual character, so J is globally defined without assuming alpha/2 is a character.

references.title: Brian Conrad and Aaron Landesman, Compact Lie Groups

items.title: The Weyl Jacobian is independent and invariant
items.statement: The Weyl Jacobian is independent of the positive system and invariant under W(G,T).

references.title: Brian Conrad and Aaron Landesman, Compact Lie Groups

items.strategy: Replacing alpha by -alpha changes |1-alpha(t)^{-1}| to |1-alpha(t)|, which is equal because |alpha(t)|=1. Any two positive systems choose one root from each ± pair, so the product is unchanged. A Weyl element permutes the unordered pairs {±alpha}, proving invariance.

items.title: Weyl integration formula
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Give G and T normalized Haar measures dg and dt, and give G/T the unique G-invariant probability measure d(xT) normalized by the Weil identity ∫_G F(x)dg=∫_{G/T}∫_T F(xt)dt d(xT). Then for every continuous f on compact connected G, ∫_G f(g)dg=(1/|W|)∫_T∫_{G/T} f(xtx^{-1})d(xT)J(t)dt; for class f the inner integral is f(t).

references.title: Brian Conrad and Aaron Landesman, Compact Lie Groups

source_locators: §15, Theorem 15.3 and proof; Appendix K for character lattices
items.strategy: Use the bi-invariant metric and the quotient submersion G→G/T. Fubini along its T-fibers gives the Weil identity for the induced invariant quotient measure; because dg and dt are probabilities, this quotient measure also has total mass one, fixing d(xT) with no hidden scalar. First take f to be a class function. On (G/T)×T_reg use q(xT,t)=xtx^{-1}; its regular fibers have exactly |W| points. In root-space coordinates its normal differential on each real root plane is 1-Ad(t), with determinant product J(t), while the quotient and torus volume forms are exactly those fixed by the Weil normalization. The singular set is the finite union of kernels of nontrivial root characters; the torus structure theorem and one-dimensional Fubini make it Haar-null. Change of variables on regular charts and the |W|-sheeted degree give the formula for class functions, and nullity extends it across the singular set. For general f, define the continuous class function f^G(g)=∫_G f(xgx^{-1})dx. Translation invariance and Fubini give ∫_G f^G=∫_G f. For t in T the integrand is right-T-invariant in x, so the Weil identity turns f^G(t) into ∫_{G/T}f(xtx^{-1})d(xT). Applying the class formula to f^G yields exactly the displayed double integral.

items.title: Character and cocharacter lattices
items.statement: For a torus T, X*(T)=Hom(T,S1) and X_*(T)=Hom(S1,T), paired by the integer n for which chi∘eta(z)=z^n.

references.title: Brian Conrad and Aaron Landesman, Compact Lie Groups

items.title: Characters are the integral weights
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. With exp normalized so exp(2pi i)=1 on S1, differentiation identifies X*(T) with the linear functionals lambda on t whose values on ker(exp) lie in 2pi i Z; the character/cocharacter pairing is perfect.

references.title: Brian Conrad and Aaron Landesman, Compact Lie Groups

items.strategy: Lift a character through t→t/Lambda: it has the form X↦exp(lambda(X)) and is well-defined exactly when lambda(Lambda)⊂2pi iZ. Conversely that condition descends the exponential. A lattice basis and its dual show both bijectivity and perfection of the integer pairing.

items.title: Root datum of a compact connected Lie group
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. A reduced compact root datum is a quadruple (X,Phi,X_vee,Phi_vee) in which X and X_vee are finite free dual lattices with a perfect integer pairing, Phi and Phi_vee are finite subsets in bijection alpha↔alpha^vee, <alpha,alpha^vee>=2, and the paired reflections s_alpha(x)=x-<x,alpha^vee>alpha and s_alpha^vee(y)=y-<alpha,y>alpha^vee preserve Phi and Phi_vee compatibly: if s_alpha(beta)=gamma, then s_alpha^vee(beta^vee)=gamma^vee. Reducedness excludes nontrivial multiples of roots. For a compact connected pair (G,T), its datum is (X*(T),Phi,X_*(T),Phi^vee), using the compact-root cocharacters supplied by the analytic Weyl theorem; central torus directions are retained even though the roots do not span them.

references.title: Brian Conrad and Aaron Landesman, Compact Lie Groups

source_locators: §21, especially Proposition 21.3 and the root-datum discussion following Remark 21.4; Appendix R §R.2

items.title: Root and weight lattice sandwich
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For compact connected semisimple G, Q⊆X*(T)⊆P. The simply connected form has character lattice P and the adjoint form has character lattice Q.

references.title: Brian Conrad and Aaron Landesman, Compact Lie Groups
Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

source_locators: Knapp Chapter IV §7, Propositions 4.58–4.68, and §8, Theorem 4.69; Chapter V §8, Theorem 5.107; Conrad–Landesman Appendix V, Theorem V.1.1
items.strategy: Roots are actual adjoint characters, giving Q⊆X*(T). Composing chi in X*(T) with each root cocharacter alpha^vee gives z↦z^{<chi,alpha^vee>}, so X*(T)⊆P. For the endpoints, first supply the missing global fact rather than assuming it: the fundamental group of a compact connected Lie group is finitely generated by a finite good-cover graph argument. If the universal-cover kernel of semisimple G were infinite, it would have finite-index subgroups of arbitrarily large index. The corresponding finite covers K are compact. Their finite central kernels lie in every maximal torus by torus containment and maximal-torus conjugacy, so restriction gives Q⊆X*(T_K)⊆P and finite character duality identifies the covering degree with [X*(T_K):X*(T)], bounded by [P:Q], a contradiction. Thus the universal cover G_sc is compact. Every dominant integral P-weight has the finite-dimensional module already constructed on DG-32; restricting its differential to the compact real Lie algebra and applying Lie's second theorem integrates it to G_sc. In particular every fundamental weight is an actual torus character, so X*(T_sc)=P. For the adjoint endpoint, write a character chi of T_ad in the real simple-root basis as sum c_i alpha_i. Let H_j be defined by alpha_i(H_j)=2pi i delta_ij. Every root has integral simple-root coordinates, so Ad(exp H_j)=1; centerlessness of the adjoint group gives exp H_j=1. Analytic integrality of chi then gives chi(H_j)=2pi i c_j in 2pi i Z, hence every c_j is integral and chi lies in Q. Thus X*(T_ad)=Q. This proves both endpoint equalities and the sandwich without presupposing the coroot lattice is the exponential kernel.

items.title: Semisimple compact groups up to isogeny
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Reduced crystallographic root systems classify compact connected semisimple Lie groups up to finite central isogeny.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

source_locators: Chapter VI §1, Theorem 6.11; §2, Corollaries 6.20–6.21; Chapter VII §1, Propositions 7.1–7.2 and Corollary 7.3
items.strategy: Cartan–Killing first constructs and identifies the complex semisimple Lie algebra g for the given root system. Reconstruct Knapp's compact-form step locally: choose normalized Chevalley root vectors and take the real span of iH_alpha, X_alpha-X_{-alpha}, and i(X_alpha+X_{-alpha}); the Chevalley bracket constants show this is a real form u, and the displayed Killing-form pairings make B|u negative definite. For uniqueness, let tau_1,tau_2 be the conjugations of two compact forms. The positive automorphism obtained from their product has a positive fourth root in Int(g_R); conjugating one involution by it makes the two commute, and a simultaneous +1/-1 eigenspace would make B both positive and negative, so the involutions coincide. Thus compact real forms are conjugate. Integrate u to its simply connected real group. Its adjoint group Int(u) is a closed subgroup of O(u,-B), hence compact, and the universal cover is compact by the finite-fundamental-group argument proved in the preceding lattice proposition. Uniqueness of simply connected integration gives one compact simply connected group for the root system. Every compact connected semisimple group with that Lie algebra is its quotient by the finite central universal-cover kernel, so any two are centrally isogenous. Conversely a finite central isogeny preserves the Lie algebra and root system. The compact-form construction is included here only for this global existence implication; no future DG-34 item is used.

items.title: Compact connected Lie groups are classified by root data
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every compact connected G, multiplication induces a finite central covering Z(G)^0×G_der^sc→G. Isomorphism classes of compact connected Lie groups (equivalently pairs with a maximal torus, modulo conjugacy) correspond to isomorphism classes of reduced compact root data, including central torus directions.

references.title: Brian Conrad and Aaron Landesman, Compact Lie Groups
Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.
Pavel Etingof, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras

source_locators: Conrad–Landesman Appendix V §V.2, printed pp. 269–270; Knapp Chapter VII §1, Propositions 7.1–7.2 and Corollary 7.3; Etingof Lecture 42, Corollaries 42.5–42.6
items.strategy: First prove the advertised cover. The invariant inner product splits g=z(g)⊕[g,g]. The connected center Z(G)^0 is the torus integrating z(g). For the compact Lie algebra [g,g], its adjoint group is a closed subgroup of an orthogonal group and its simply connected integration G_der^sc is compact by the preceding semisimple argument. Lie's second theorem integrates the inclusion [g,g]→g to G_der^sc→G. Multiplication Z(G)^0×G_der^sc→G has an isomorphism on Lie algebras, hence open image; connectedness makes it surjective. Its kernel is discrete in the connected compact domain, hence finite and central. Now reconstruct from a root datum. In X_Q split off the rational root span and its central complement, the annihilator of the coroot span. The semisimple root system determines G_der^sc, whose torus character lattice is P; the projected central lattice determines a torus A. The datum embeds X as a finite-index sublattice of X*(A×T_sc), and finite character duality recovers the finite subgroup C as the common kernel of X. Since Q⊆X, C annihilates every root and is central in A×G_der^sc. The quotient (A×G_der^sc)/C has exactly the prescribed roots, coroots, and paired lattices. An isomorphism of root data respects the based root system, including diagram automorphisms; the normalized-root-vector isomorphism and compact-form uniqueness lift it to G_der^sc, while lattice duality lifts its central part to A and carries C to C'. It therefore descends to a group isomorphism. Conversely a group isomorphism carries a maximal torus to one conjugate to the chosen torus and induces a root-datum isomorphism. This proves essential surjectivity and both directions of the isomorphism classification rather than citing Conrad §28, whose Remark 21.4 explicitly leaves the classification proof outside that course. The finite-cover clause is now a proof-bearing supplier for compact highest weights and the Weyl formula.

items.title: Central quotients and intermediate character lattices
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a simply connected compact semisimple group G_sc, a maximal torus T_sc, and the quotient markings G_sc→G_sc/C. Central subgroups C⊆Z(G_sc) correspond contravariantly to lattices X with Q⊆X⊆P. If the markings are forgotten, abstract isomorphism classes are the orbits of these subgroups, equivalently of the intermediate lattices, under root-datum (Dynkin-diagram) automorphisms.

references.title: Brian Conrad and Aaron Landesman, Compact Lie Groups

items.strategy: For a central subgroup C of G_sc (automatically finite), the characters of T_sc/C are exactly weights in P trivial on C, an intermediate lattice X. Inclusion of central subgroups reverses inclusion of annihilator lattices. Perfect finite character duality recovers C as the common kernel of X, proving the bijection for marked quotient maps. If G_sc/C_1 and G_sc/C_2 are abstractly isomorphic, lift the isomorphism uniquely to the simply connected covers; the lift is an automorphism carrying C_1 to C_2. Inner automorphisms act trivially on the center, while outer automorphisms induce the Dynkin/root-datum action. Thus forgetting the marking requires taking those automorphism orbits, exactly as warned in Conrad–Landesman Appendix V §V.2.

items.title: Left and right regular representations on L2(G)
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. On the Hilbert space L2(G,dg), define (L_x f)(y)=f(x^{-1}y) and (R_x f)(y)=f(yx); Haar invariance makes both actions unitary.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.title: Convolution operators
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For k in C(G), set (T_k f)(x)=∫_G k(x^{-1}y)f(y)dy; this fixes the right-convolution convention used below.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.title: Continuous convolution operators are Hilbert–Schmidt
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For k in C(G), T_k has square-integrable kernel K(x,y)=k(x^{-1}y), is Hilbert–Schmidt, and is compact.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: Haar invariance gives ∫_{G×G}|k(x^{-1}y)|^2 dxdy=||k||_2^2<∞. The L2-kernel theorem identifies T_k as Hilbert–Schmidt, and the authored Hilbert–Schmidt compactness theorem makes it compact.

items.title: Spectral convolution eigenspaces are finite-dimensional and invariant
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. If k*=k, then T_k is compact self-adjoint with finite-dimensional nonzero eigenspaces invariant under the left regular representation and with range closure equal to their Hilbert direct sum. For arbitrary k, the same conclusions apply to the positive operator T_k* T_k.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: The adjoint kernel calculation gives T_k*=T_{k*} with k*(x)=overline{k(x^{-1})}; hence Hermitian k gives a compact self-adjoint T_k, while arbitrary k gives positive compact T_k*T_k. Directly changing variables in the convolution formula shows these operators commute with all L_g. The compact self-adjoint spectral theorem gives finite-dimensional nonzero eigenspaces and their orthogonal expansion of the range closure. Commutation makes each eigenspace L_g-invariant.

items.title: Central continuous approximate identities
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For compact Lie G, C(G) is dense in L2(G), and both translation actions are strongly continuous on L2(G). There are nonnegative continuous central inversion-invariant functions k_n of Haar integral one, supported in shrinking identity neighborhoods, such that T_{k_n}f→f uniformly for f in C(G) and T_{k_n}H→H in L2 for H in L2(G); T_kH is continuous whenever k is continuous and H is in L2. Closed translation-invariant subspaces are stable under these convolution averages, and conjugation/inversion averages preserve them when the corresponding symmetries do.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

source_locators: Chapter IV §3, the density paragraph and Lemmas 4.17–4.19
items.strategy: Because compact G is LCH and normalized Haar is Radon, the cited C_c-density theorem gives C(G)=C_c(G) dense in L2(G). Translations are L2-isometries; approximate H by a continuous c and use uniform continuity of c to prove ||L_xH-H||_2 and ||R_xH-H||_2 tend to zero at the identity, exactly Knapp Lemma 4.17. For radii r_n→0 take b_n(x)=max(0,1-d(e,x)/r_n). Bi-invariance makes b_n central and inversion-invariant; positivity of Haar on nonempty opens makes its integral positive, so normalize to k_n. Uniform continuity proves uniform convergence on C(G), while Minkowski's integral inequality and strong translation continuity give ||T_{k_n}H-H||_2≤sup_{y in supp(k_n)}||R_yH-H||_2→0. Cauchy–Schwarz and L2-continuity of translates of k show T_kH is continuous. Finally Knapp Lemmas 4.18–4.19 approximate every such convolution in L2 by finite linear combinations of translates of H. Hence a closed translation-invariant subspace contains the convolution; the identical scalar-pairing/Fubini argument handles conjugation averages, and inversion is an L2-isometry. This supplies every closure assertion later used for U and U^perp.

items.title: Peter–Weyl theorem
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. The normalized matrix coefficients sqrt(dim pi) pi_ij, over inequivalent irreducible unitary representations, form an orthonormal Hilbert basis of L2(G); the pi-isotypic left-regular summand has multiplicity dim pi.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

source_locators: Chapter IV §3, Lemmas 4.17–4.19, Theorem 4.20, and Corollary 4.21
items.strategy: Schur orthogonality gives the stated orthonormal family. Let U be its closed span; the explicit formulas for translating and inverting a matrix coefficient make U, and hence U^perp, stable under left/right translations, inversion, conjugation, and conjugate-linear involution. If U^perp contains nonzero H, the preceding strong-continuity/approximate-identity lemma gives T_{k_n}H→H in L2, makes each T_{k_n}H continuous, and keeps it in U^perp; choose a nonzero F_1. Translate and rotate its phase so F_1(e) is real and nonzero, average y↦F_1(yxy^{-1}) over conjugacy, and set F(x)=F_2(x)+overline{F_2(x^{-1})}. The preceding stability lemma keeps F in U^perp, while F(e)=2F_1(e)≠0; F is continuous, central, and Hermitian. Thus T_F is a nonzero compact self-adjoint convolution. A nonzero-eigenvalue eigenspace is finite-dimensional and left-invariant; unitarity and complete reducibility give an irreducible summand W with orthonormal basis f_i. Its regular-action coefficients h_ii lie in U. Fubini, centrality, and the convolution convention give <F,h_ii>=<T_Ff_i,f_i>=lambda, contradicting F⊥U. Hence U=L2. For a d-dimensional irreducible pi, the d column spaces are mutually orthogonal equivalent left copies, and Schur orthogonality exhausts its isotypic component, proving multiplicity d.

items.title: Matrix coefficients are uniformly dense in C(G)
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Finite linear combinations of finite-dimensional unitary matrix coefficients are uniformly dense in C(G).

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: Given f and epsilon, first choose k_n with ||f*k_n-f||_infty<epsilon/2. Approximate k_n in L2 by a finite Peter–Weyl sum p. Cauchy–Schwarz gives ||f*(k_n-p)||_infty<=||f||_2||k_n-p||_2, so f*p is uniformly close and is a finite matrix-coefficient sum. For the independent Stone–Weierstrass check, coefficients contain constants and are closed under products and conjugation. They separate x from y: otherwise every irreducible has pi(y^{-1}x)=I, so left translation by y^{-1}x fixes the dense Peter–Weyl span and hence all L2(G), contradicting a continuous bump supported in an identity neighborhood disjoint from its translate. Complex Stone–Weierstrass then gives the same uniform closure without a forward dependency.

items.title: Finite-dimensional representations separate points
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For distinct x,y in a compact Lie group, some finite-dimensional unitary representation pi satisfies pi(x)≠pi(y).

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: Choose a continuous function f with f(x)≠f(y). Uniformly approximate it closely enough by a finite sum of matrix coefficients. Some summand has different values at x and y, so its underlying representation distinguishes the points.

items.title: Every compact Lie group is a closed matrix group
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every compact Lie group has a faithful finite-dimensional unitary representation and hence is isomorphic to a closed subgroup of U(N).

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: Choose a no-small-subgroups neighborhood U of the identity. For every x in compact G\U, separation gives a finite-dimensional representation nontrivial at x, and continuity gives a neighborhood on which it is nontrivial. A finite subcover yields finitely many representations; their direct sum has kernel contained in U. Its kernel is a subgroup, hence trivial. The injective continuous homomorphism from compact G has compact, therefore closed, image in U(N).

items.title: Highest weights for compact connected groups
