items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For compact connected G with maximal torus T and chosen positive roots, irreducible finite-dimensional complex representations are classified by the dominant elements of the actual character lattice X*(T).

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: Differentiate an irreducible G-module. The central torus acts by a character by Schur's lemma, and the complexified derived algebra has a dominant highest weight; restriction to T makes the combined weight an element of X*(T). Conversely use the proved finite central cover p:Z(G)^0×G_der^sc→G. Pull lambda back to its maximal torus. Its central component is a character of Z(G)^0, while its semisimple component lies in P and gives the algebraic highest-weight representation, uniquely integrated to the simply connected compact derived factor. Every element of ker p is central, so it acts on this irreducible product module by the scalar obtained by evaluating the pulled-back highest character; because lambda came from X*(T), that scalar is one. The module therefore descends to G. Connectedness makes differentiation faithful on intertwiners, so the two constructions are inverse and preserve irreducibility. This explicitly uses the full central-torus-times-derived cover, not merely the derived universal cover.

items.title: Differentiation and integration of highest weights
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Differentiation sends a compact-group highest weight to the same highest weight for the complexified derived Lie algebra; a compatible Lie-algebra module integrates to G exactly when its torus weights lie in X*(T), equivalently when the finite central covering kernel acts trivially.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: Differentiate the T-eigencharacter on the highest line to obtain its t-weight; root subgroup differentials preserve the chosen positive system. Integration on the simply connected derived cover is unique. A representation descends through the central cover precisely when its kernel acts trivially, and evaluation of central elements on weight spaces is exactly the character-lattice condition.

items.title: Weyl denominator and anti-invariant orbit sums
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. On the maximal torus of the finite central cover Z(G)^0×G_der^sc, rho is a character and A_rho=sum_w det(w)e^{w rho}=e^rho product_{alpha>0}(1-e^{-alpha}); moreover the alternating orbit sums A_nu for strictly dominant nu form a triangular Z-basis of Weyl anti-invariants.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: On the simply connected derived torus, fundamental weights and hence rho are characters; extend trivially across the central torus. Both sides of the denominator identity are anti-invariant under each simple reflection: the product changes sign after the single alpha_i factor is reversed. Their leading term in dominance order is e^rho with coefficient one, and every other term lies below. Subtracting leaves an anti-invariant supported strictly below rho. Each regular Weyl orbit has a unique strictly dominant representative and each singular orbit sum cancels; but a strictly dominant integral weight is sum m_i omega_i with every m_i≥1, while rho=sum omega_i, so none lies strictly below rho. The difference is therefore zero. The same orbit-by-orbit cancellation says any anti-invariant has constant signed coefficients on a regular orbit and zero coefficients on a singular orbit, giving the A_nu basis and triangularity. No individual half-root is asserted to be a character of T.

items.title: Orthogonality identifies the Weyl numerator
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For dominant lambda in X*(T), on the central cover one has A_rho chi_lambda=A_{lambda+rho}.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: The highest-weight triangularity and the denominator lemma make A_rho chi_lambda an anti-invariant whose leading orbit sum is A_{lambda+rho}; expand the remainder in lower A_{mu+rho}. Weyl integration rewrites <chi_lambda,chi_mu>_G as |W|^{-1}<A_rho chi_lambda,A_rho chi_mu>_T because |A_rho|^2=J. Character orthogonality and orthogonality of distinct torus characters make the lower coefficients vanish inductively over dominance order, while the leading coefficient is one. This proves the numerator identity locally, without importing a character formula.

items.title: Weyl character formula for compact connected groups
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For dominant lambda in X*(T) and regular t in T, chi_lambda(t)=A_{lambda+rho}(tilde t)/A_rho(tilde t) for any lift tilde t to the maximal torus of Z(G)^0×G_der^sc; the quotient is lift-independent and extends uniquely and continuously to every t in T.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: Divide the proved numerator identity on the regular set, where the denominator product is nonzero. If two lifts differ by a finite central-kernel element z, lambda(z)=1 and w(rho)-rho lies in the root lattice, whose characters are trivial on z; numerator and denominator therefore acquire the same scalar e^rho(z), so their quotient agrees and descends. The descended quotient equals the already continuous character on the dense regular set. Defining its values at singular points by that character gives the unique continuous extension. This uses the full cover Z(G)^0×G_der^sc and never assumes rho or alpha/2 lies in X*(T).

items.title: Dominant characters form the representation-ring basis
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. The character map embeds R(G) into Z[X*(T)]^W, and the irreducible characters indexed by dominant weights form its Z-basis; multiplication corresponds to tensor product.

references.title: Brian Conrad and Aaron Landesman, Compact Lie Groups

items.strategy: Complete reducibility makes the Grothendieck group free on irreducible classes, and character additivity/multiplicativity sends direct sums/tensor products to sums/products. Orthogonality makes irreducible characters linearly independent. Highest-weight classification supplies exactly one for every dominant actual character, and restriction to T is W-invariant; hence these are the asserted basis.

items.title: Compact Haar measure is bi-invariant
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Normalized Haar measure on a compact group is only left invariant, not right invariant.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: For any h, E↦mu(Eh) is another normalized left-invariant measure. Uniqueness makes it equal to mu, so right invariance holds.

items.title: Disconnected elements need not lie in identity-component tori
items.statement: Every element of a disconnected compact Lie group lies in a maximal torus of its identity component.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: In the compact zero-dimensional group Z/2, the identity component and its only torus are {e}; the nonidentity element lies outside it.

items.title: Root systems determine only isogeny class
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. A root system determines a compact connected semisimple group up to isomorphism.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: SU(2) and SO(3) have root system A1 but different centers and fundamental groups, so they are not isomorphic. They are related by a finite central isogeny.

items.title: Not every abstract dominant weight integrates
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every dominant weight in the abstract weight lattice integrates to every compact group form with the given Lie algebra.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: For SO(3), the actual character lattice is the A1 root lattice, so the fundamental weight is dominant in P but does not descend from SU(2).

items.title: Peter–Weyl gives density, not finite equality
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every continuous function on a compact Lie group is a finite sum of matrix coefficients.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: On S1 the matrix coefficients are Laurent monomials, so finite sums are trigonometric polynomials. The continuous function theta↦|sin theta| has infinitely many nonzero Fourier coefficients and is not a trigonometric polynomial, although such polynomials approximate it uniformly.

items.title: Compact groups have infinite-dimensional unitary representations
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every unitary representation of a compact group is finite-dimensional.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: For an infinite compact Lie group such as S1, L2(G) is infinite-dimensional and the left regular action is unitary. Peter–Weyl decomposes it into finite-dimensional pieces but does not make the whole space finite-dimensional.

title: Compact Lie Groups Maximal Tori and Peter Weyl Theory — Examples

items.title: Normalized Haar measure on a torus
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Under T^r=(R/Z)^r, normalized Haar integration is integration over [0,1)^r with Lebesgue measure.

references.title: Brian Conrad and Aaron Landesman, Compact Lie Groups

items.strategy: Translation invariance modulo Z^r follows from partitioning and translating a fundamental cube; total mass is one. Uniqueness of normalized Haar identifies this measure.

items.title: Maximal tori and Weyl groups of U(n) and SU(n)
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. The diagonal unitary matrices form a maximal torus of U(n), their determinant-one part a maximal torus of SU(n), and both Weyl groups are S_n acting by coordinate permutation.

references.title: Brian Conrad and Aaron Landesman, Compact Lie Groups

items.strategy: Commuting normal matrices are simultaneously unitarily diagonalizable, so no larger connected abelian subgroup exists. Permutation matrices normalize the diagonal torus and realize S_n. A normalizer must permute the common one-dimensional eigenspaces of a regular diagonal element; modulo diagonal matrices it is a permutation matrix. Adjust determinant in SU(n) by a diagonal factor.

items.title: A maximal torus and Weyl group of SO(3)
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Rotations about a fixed axis form a maximal torus S1 in SO(3), and its Weyl group has order two, acting by angle reversal.

references.title: Brian Conrad and Aaron Landesman, Compact Lie Groups

items.strategy: A connected commuting family of rotations fixes a common axis, giving maximality. A half-turn about a perpendicular axis normalizes the torus and reverses its angle. Any normalizer preserves the fixed axis as an unoriented line; modulo rotations about it, only the two orientations remain.

items.title: Weyl integration for SU(2)
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a continuous class function f on SU(2), its integral is (1/2) times the circle integral f(diag(z,z^{-1}))|1-z^{-2}|^2 dz.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: The maximal torus is diag(z,z^{-1}), W has order two, and the positive root character is z↦z^2. Substitute |W|=2 and J(z)=|1-z^{-2}|^2 into the general formula.

items.title: Character lattices of SU(2) and SO(3)
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For type A1, X*(T_SU2)=P=Z omega while X*(T_SO3)=Q=2Z omega; precisely the even SU(2) highest weights descend to SO(3).

references.title: Brian Conrad and Aaron Landesman, Compact Lie Groups

items.strategy: Parametrize T_SU2 by diag(z,z^{-1}); z^n gives weight n omega. The kernel {±I} of SU(2)→SO(3) is killed exactly when n is even, so the quotient character lattice is 2Z omega=Q.

items.title: Simply connected, adjoint, and intermediate compact forms
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a semisimple compact root system, the simply connected form corresponds to P, the adjoint form to Q, and intermediate central quotients to intermediate lattices Q⊆X⊆P.

references.title: Brian Conrad and Aaron Landesman, Compact Lie Groups

items.strategy: Start with G_sc. For C≤Z(G_sc), characters of T_sc/C are the annihilator of C in P. The trivial C yields P, the full center yields Q, and finite character duality pairs intermediate central subgroups with all intermediate lattices, reversing inclusion.

items.title: Fourier series on a torus as Peter–Weyl
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For T^r, the irreducible unitary representations are the characters x↦e^{2pi i<n,x>} for n in Z^r, and Peter–Weyl is the usual Fourier orthonormal basis theorem.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: Commutativity and Schur's lemma make every irreducible finite-dimensional unitary representation one-dimensional. The character lattice computation lists them by Z^r. Peter–Weyl therefore gives exactly the standard exponential basis and Parseval expansion.

items.title: Matrix coefficients of the standard SU(2) representation
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Writing g=[[a,b],[-conj(b),conj(a)]], the four coordinate functions a,b,-conj(b),conj(a) are the matrix coefficients of the standard two-dimensional representation and are orthogonal with squared norm 1/2.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: Use the standard orthonormal basis of C^2: the entries are exactly <ge_j,e_i>. The representation is irreducible because no complex line is fixed by all SU(2) matrices. Schur orthogonality with dimension two gives pairwise orthogonality and norm square 1/2.

items.title: Finite-group Schur orthogonality
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a finite group, normalized Haar measure is counting measure divided by |G|, and compact Schur orthogonality becomes the usual finite-group matrix-coefficient formula.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: A finite group is a zero-dimensional compact Lie group, and normalized counting measure is its unique Haar probability. Replacing the Haar integral by |G|^{-1}sum_g in the exact formula gives classical Schur orthogonality.

items.title: SU(2) and SO(3) share roots but are not isomorphic
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. SU(2) and SO(3) have the same A1 root system and are centrally isogenous, but are not isomorphic.

references.title: Brian Conrad and Aaron Landesman, Compact Lie Groups

items.strategy: The adjoint double cover SU(2)→SO(3) identifies their Lie algebras and roots. SU(2) has center {±I}, whereas SO(3) has trivial center; an isomorphism preserves centers. Their differing character lattices record the same obstruction.

items.title: A disconnected element outside every identity-component torus
items.statement: In O(2), any reflection lies outside SO(2)=O(2)^0 and hence outside every torus contained in the identity component.

references.title: Brian Conrad and Aaron Landesman, Compact Lie Groups

items.strategy: Determinant is continuous with values ±1. Every connected subgroup containing the identity has determinant +1, whereas a reflection has determinant -1. Therefore no identity-component torus contains it.

items.title: Peter–Weyl decomposition of L2(SU(2))
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. As an SU(2)×SU(2) module, L2(SU(2)) is the Hilbert direct sum over n>=0 of V(n) tensor V(n)*; under the left action alone, V(n) occurs with multiplicity n+1.

references.title: Anthony W. Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, 2nd ed.

items.strategy: The matrix-coefficient space of V(n) is canonically V(n)* tensor V(n), with left and right translations acting on the two factors. Schur orthogonality makes distinct n orthogonal and Peter–Weyl makes their Hilbert sum exhaustive. Since dim V(n)=n+1, forgetting the right action leaves n+1 copies under the left action.
